props.title: Easter Parade
props.initialSlug: Musical duo finds love amid showbiz rivalry

sections.content: Easter Parade (1948) stands as one of MGM's most dazzling Technicolor musicals, pairing Fred Astaire and Judy Garland at the height of their powers. After Ann Miller's character leaves his act, Astaire's Don Hewes boldly claims he can transform any chorus girl into a star - leading to Garland's transformation from unknown performer to sensation. The film marked a crucial moment in musical cinema, bridging the gap between the elegant ballroom style of Astaire's earlier works like Top Hat (1935) and the more contemporary American musical emerging in films like On The Town (1949). Irving Berlin's score delivers 17 unforgettable numbers, including "Steppin' Out With My Baby" and the titular "Easter Parade."

sections.content: The late 1940s represented a golden age for MGM musicals, with producer Arthur Freed assembling an unmatched roster of talent. While Easter Parade maintained traditional musical elements, films like The Pirate (1948) and Words and Music (1948) began experimenting with more integrated storytelling approaches. Notably, Easter Parade was originally planned for Gene Kelly, but an ankle injury led to Astaire coming out of his brief retirement - a fortunate accident that gave us one of Hollywood's most magical screen partnerships. SUBHEAD: The Irving Berlin Connection

Irving Berlin's contribution to Easter Parade goes beyond just providing songs - the film represents the perfect marriage of Berlin's Tin Pan Alley sensibilities with MGM's production values. The integration of period songs like "When That Midnight Choo-Choo Leaves for Alabam'" alongside new compositions showed how musicals could blend nostalgia with contemporary appeal. This approach influenced later period musicals like Meet Me in St. Louis (1944) and The Harvey Girls (1946), both also starring Garland.
